formal_definition: A mathematical model for data types in which a data type is defined by its behavior (semantics) from the point of view of a user of the data, specifically in terms of possible values, possible operations on data of this type, and the behavior of these operations. This contrasts with data structures, which are concrete representations of data from the point of view of an implementer rather than a user.
student_friendly_explanation: An abstract data type is like a blueprint for how to use data, telling you what kind of data you can work with and what actions you can perform on that data without needing to know how it's actually stored.
example: A stack, where you can push items onto it and pop them off, is an example of an abstract data type.
related_terms: Data Structure; Object-Oriented Programming; Software Design

formal_definition: A subfield of artificial intelligence in which systems learn patterns from data and improve their performance on a task without being explicitly programmed for every rule.
student_friendly_explanation: Machine Learning is like teaching a computer to learn from examples instead of following strict rules. It helps computers get better at tasks by learning from data.
example: Google's spam filter uses Machine Learning to learn what emails are spam and what are not, improving its accuracy over time.

formal_definition: A software bug where a program fails to release memory it no longer needs, gradually consuming more resources over time and potentially degrading performance or crashing.
student_friendly_explanation: A memory leak happens when a program doesn't give back the space it uses for storing data, so it keeps using more and more of the computer's memory, which can slow down the computer or make it crash.
example: Imagine you have a toy box that gets smaller every day but never empties. If you don't put away the toys you're done playing with, the toy box will keep getting smaller and smaller until there's nothing left.
related_terms: Garbage Collection; Resource Management; Resource Allocation

formal_definition: Data that describes other data, such as a file's creation date, author, or format, providing context without being part of the primary content itself.
student_friendly_explanation: Metadata is like when you write down who wrote a book and when it was written, but instead, we use it to describe information about digital files like what software they were made with or who created them.
example: When you open a PDF file, metadata might tell you who created the document and when it was last edited.

formal_definition: Software that acts as a bridge between different applications or between an operating system and applications, handling communication and data management between them.
student_friendly_explanation: Middleware is like a helper between different computer programs. It makes sure they can talk to each other smoothly and share information easily.
example: A chat application uses middleware to connect with servers, allowing users to send messages without needing to know all the details about how the servers work.

formal_definition: A technique where a program executes multiple threads concurrently within a single process, allowing tasks to run in parallel and make better use of processor resources.
student_friendly_explanation: Multithreading is like having several cooks in the kitchen who can prepare different dishes at the same time, using the same stove and ingredients, so you get food faster.
example: A web browser uses multithreading to handle multiple tabs or windows simultaneously, allowing you to browse, search, and interact with websites without slowing down.

formal_definition: A container that provides context for identifiers, allowing the same name to be used in different namespaces without conflict, commonly used to organize code.
student_friendly_explanation: A namespace is like a special box where you keep names for things, so you can use the same name for different things without them getting mixed up. It's used to organize code and make sure everything works correctly.
example: When you write a program, you might have a function named 'print'. In one part of your code, you want to print something, and in another part, you want to do something else with 'print'. Namespaces help you use the same name 'print' without confusing them.

formal_definition: A computing system loosely inspired by the human brain, made up of layers of interconnected nodes that learn to recognize patterns by adjusting connection weights during training.
student_friendly_explanation: A neural network is like a brain of a computer that learns how to recognize things, just like you do! It has layers of nodes that connect and adjust based on what it sees, helping it get better at recognizing patterns over time.
example: Neural networks are used in self-driving cars to help them understand and react to their environment.
related_terms: Machine Learning; Deep Learning; Pattern Recognition

formal_definition: The practice of distributing computing workloads across multiple servers or resources to optimize performance, maximize throughput, and avoid overloading any single resource.
student_friendly_explanation: Load balancing is like sharing your toys equally among friends so no one gets too many or too few. It helps computers share tasks fairly to keep everything running smoothly.
example: When you visit a website, load balancers make sure that different parts of the site are handled by different servers, which speeds up loading times and keeps the site running well.

formal_definition: The process of organizing a relational database's tables and columns to reduce data redundancy and improve data integrity, typically by splitting data into related tables.
student_friendly_explanation: Normalization is like sorting your toys so that each toy has its own special spot in your room. This helps keep everything organized and makes it easier to find what you need.
example: Imagine you have a table for customers with their addresses mixed in. By normalizing, you split the address into separate tables for customer names and addresses, making sure no information is lost and making it simpler to manage.
related_terms: Relational Model; Data Integrity; Database Schema

formal_definition: Software whose source code is made publicly available for anyone to view, use, modify, and distribute, usually under a license that governs how it can be reused.
student_friendly_explanation: Open Source means the code for software programs is freely shared and can be changed by anyone. It's like having a recipe book where everyone can see and improve the recipes.
example: Many popular applications like Firefox and WordPress are open source, allowing developers to work together to make them better.

formal_definition: System software that manages computer hardware and software resources and provides common services for computer programs, sitting between applications and the hardware.
student_friendly_explanation: An operating system is like a helper that talks to your computer's hardware and makes sure all the programs can work together smoothly. It acts as an interface between you and the computer.
example: Imagine you have a toy box where you keep all your toys. An operating system is like a toy organizer that helps you find and play with your toys more easily.

formal_definition: A modeling error in machine learning where a model learns the training data too closely, including its noise, resulting in poor performance on new, unseen data.
student_friendly_explanation: Overfitting is when a machine learning model remembers the training data so well that it starts to remember the noise instead of the actual pattern. This makes it hard for the model to make good predictions on new data.
example: A model trained to recognize cats in photos might start to classify every small, dark spot as a cat, even if it's just a shadow or a piece of lint.

formal_definition: A formatted unit of data carried by a packet-switched network, containing both the payload being transmitted and control information such as source and destination addresses.
student_friendly_explanation: A packet is like a letter that contains your message and also includes information about where to send it and how to find you.
example: When you send an email, your computer breaks down the message into small packets and sends them over the internet to reach your friend's computer.

formal_definition: A type of computation in which many calculations or processes are carried out simultaneously, often by splitting a large problem into smaller ones solved at the same time.
student_friendly_explanation: Parallel computing is like working on different parts of a big puzzle at the same time. Imagine you have a huge jigsaw puzzle and you split it into smaller sections to finish faster.
example: Parallel computing is used in video game servers where multiple players can interact simultaneously without slowing down the game.

formal_definition: The process of analyzing a sequence of symbols, such as source code or text, according to the rules of a formal grammar to determine its structure.
student_friendly_explanation: Parsing is like reading a recipe and understanding how to make a dish. It's about breaking down instructions into smaller parts to see what they mean.
example: When you write a program in a programming language, parsing helps the computer understand your instructions and turn them into something it can execute.

formal_definition: A decentralized network architecture in which participating computers, called peers, share resources directly with each other without relying on a central server.
student_friendly_explanation: Peer-to-peer networks are like a group of friends sharing toys and games without needing a teacher to organize them. Each computer in the network shares its files and resources with others directly, just like how you might lend your books to your friends.
example: Sharing music files among friends on a home network without using a music streaming service.
related_terms: Network Architecture; Client-Server Model; File Sharing

formal_definition: A programming paradigm based on the concept of objects, which bundle data and behavior together, supporting principles like encapsulation, inheritance, and polymorphism.
student_friendly_explanation: Object-Oriented Programming is a way to write code that groups data and functions into 'objects'. Think of it like making a recipe book where each recipe (object) has its own ingredients (data) and steps (functions). This helps keep things organized and makes it easier to change recipes later.
example: Creating a class for a car object that includes properties like color and speed, and methods to accelerate or brake.

formal_definition: In object-oriented programming, the ability of different classes to be treated as instances of the same general type through a shared interface, while behaving differently.
student_friendly_explanation: Polymorphism is like being able to use a magic wand that works differently depending on what you wave it over - it can change its behavior based on what it's pointing at.
example: When you have a function that can work with different types of objects, like a method that sorts items, and you can pass in lists of numbers, strings, or even custom objects that implement the sorting logic, that's polymorphism in action.

formal_definition: A linear data structure where each element, called a node, points to the next node in the sequence, allowing efficient insertion and deletion without shifting elements.
student_friendly_explanation: A linked list is like a chain where each link (node) points to the next one. It's great for adding or removing items without moving others.
example: When you're building a playlist on Spotify, each song can be seen as a node in a linked list, with each node pointing to the next song.

formal_definition: A type of database that stores data as a simple collection of key and value pairs, optimized for fast lookups rather than complex relational queries.
student_friendly_explanation: A key-value store is like a big dictionary where you can quickly find information using a unique key, just like looking up a word in a dictionary.
example: Amazon's DynamoDB uses key-value stores to efficiently manage and retrieve large amounts of data.

formal_definition: In computer programming, a variable with global scope, meaning that it is visible and accessible throughout the program unless shadowed.
student_friendly_explanation: A global variable is like a shared toy box where everyone in the playground can use the same toys. It's available everywhere in the game, not just in one area.
example: In a game where you can collect coins anywhere, the total number of coins collected by all players would be a global variable.

formal_definition: The study of graphs, mathematical structures used to model pairwise relations between objects, made up of vertices connected by edges.
student_friendly_explanation: Graph Theory is about studying how things are connected, like drawing dots (vertices) and lines (edges) to show relationships between items.
example: A social network can be represented as a graph where people are dots and friendships are lines connecting them.

formal_definition: A function that can be used to map data of arbitrary size to data of a fixed size, often used with a hash table to accelerate data lookup.
student_friendly_explanation: A hash function is like a magical box that takes any piece of information and squishes it into a small number. This helps computers quickly find what they're looking for, just like how you might use a key to open a specific drawer.
example: When you search for a product on an e-commerce website, the hash function helps the computer find the product's details much faster than if it had to check every item.
related_terms: Hash Table; Data Structure; Database Index

formal_definition: A data structure that implements an associative array abstract data type, using a hash function to compute an index into an array of buckets from which a value can be found.
student_friendly_explanation: A hash table is like a magical storage box where you can quickly find anything you put in. It uses a special trick called a hash function to know exactly where to put and get things.
example: When you use a search engine, it uses hash tables to quickly find information about what you're looking for.

formal_definition: A specialized tree-based data structure which is essentially an almost complete tree satisfying the heap property regarding parent and child node values.
student_friendly_explanation: A heap is like a special kind of tree where each parent node is smaller (or larger) than its children. It's used to quickly find the smallest or largest item.
example: When organizing tasks based on urgency, you might use a max-heap where the most urgent task is always at the top.

formal_definition: Research into the design and use of computer technology, focused on the interfaces between people and computers, situated at the intersection of computer science, behavioral sciences, and design.
student_friendly_explanation: Human-Computer Interaction is about how we make computers easier to use by designing better ways for people to interact with them. It's where computer scientists, psychologists, and designers work together to create more intuitive tech.
example: Designing touchscreens for smartphones that are easy to use even for people who aren't tech-savvy.

formal_definition: In computer languages, tokens which name language entities such as variables, types, labels, subroutines, and packages.
student_friendly_explanation: An identifier is like a name you give to something in a computer program, like a variable or a function. It helps the computer know what you're talking about.
example: In a program, you might use an identifier like 'userAge' to store how old someone is.

formal_definition: The delay between a request being made and the corresponding response being received, often measured in milliseconds in networking and computing contexts.
student_friendly_explanation: Latency is like the time it takes for your computer to respond after you ask it a question. It's important because faster responses make things feel more responsive.
example: When you type a website address into your browser and see the page load almost instantly, that quick response time is due to low latency.

formal_definition: A programming paradigm that uses statements that change a program's state, focused on describing how a program operates through commands.
student_friendly_explanation: Imperative programming is like giving step-by-step instructions to a robot to do something. You tell it what to do and how to do it, bit by bit.
example: Creating a simple calculator that adds two numbers together, where each number is inputted and then added using specific commands.

formal_definition: The communication between an information processing system, such as a computer, and the outside world, involving signals or data received and sent.
student_friendly_explanation: Input/Output is how a computer talks to the outside world. It's like when you tell a friend what game you want to play, or when your friend tells you what game they have.
example: When you type something on your keyboard or see something appear on your screen, that's input/output at work.

formal_definition: A simple sorting algorithm that builds the final sorted array or list one item at a time.
student_friendly_explanation: Insertion Sort is like putting cards in order by hand. You take one card at a time and find its right spot in the already sorted part of the deck.
example: Imagine you have a bunch of playing cards out of order on a table, and you want to sort them from lowest to highest. You start with the first card, then move to the second, and so on, always placing each card in its correct position among the previously sorted cards.
related_terms: Sorting Algorithm; Bubble Sort; Merge Sort

formal_definition: A software application that provides comprehensive facilities to computer programmers for software development, normally consisting of a source code editor, build automation tools, and a debugger.
student_friendly_explanation: An Integrated Development Environment (IDE) is like a special tool that helps programmers write, test, and fix their computer programs more easily. It has features like a place to type code, tools to help make sure the code works correctly, and a way to find and fix mistakes.
example: A programmer uses an IDE to write a new app, check if it works as expected, and fix any bugs before sharing it with others.
related_terms: Source Code Editor; Build Automation Tools; Debugger

formal_definition: The phase in software testing in which individual software modules are combined and tested as a group, occurring after unit testing and before validation testing.
student_friendly_explanation: Integration Testing is when we put together different parts of a program that were tested separately earlier to make sure they work well together.
example: Imagine you have three small games on your phone: a puzzle game, a racing game, and a card game. Integration Testing would be like putting all three games together to make sure they can talk to each other and don't crash or have bugs.
related_terms: Unit Testing; Validation Testing; System Testing

formal_definition: A high-level, interpreted programming language originally built for adding interactivity to web pages, now also widely used on servers through runtimes like Node.js.
student_friendly_explanation: JavaScript is a special kind of computer language that helps make websites more interactive and fun. It's like giving life to static web pages so they can respond to user actions.
example: When you click a button on a website and it changes color or shows a message, JavaScript is what makes that happen.

formal_definition: A database operation that combines rows from two or more tables based on a related column between them, commonly used to pull related data together in a single query.
student_friendly_explanation: Join is like combining different pieces of a puzzle to see the whole picture. It helps us get information from different parts of a database by matching similar data.
example: Imagine you have a table of customers and another table of orders. By using a join, you can find out which customer made each order.

formal_definition: The core component of an operating system, managing communication between hardware and software, handling memory, processes, and device control at the lowest level.
student_friendly_explanation: The kernel is like the brain of your computer's operating system. It talks to your hardware, like your keyboard and mouse, and makes sure all the parts work together smoothly.
example: When you press a key on your keyboard, the kernel sends that information to the appropriate program so you can see what you typed on the screen.

formal_definition: In object-oriented programming, the mechanism of basing an object or class upon another object or class, retaining similar implementation and forming a hierarchy of classes.
student_friendly_explanation: Inheritance is like building a new toy car from an old one. You keep the same parts and design but add some new features. It helps create a family of similar objects or classes.
example: Creating a 'Vehicle' class and then making 'Car' and 'Motorcycle' inherit from it, both sharing methods like 'startEngine' and 'stopEngine'.

formal_definition: A term used to describe the concept that flawed or nonsense input data produces nonsense output, and can also refer to poorly written programs producing nonsensical behavior.
student_friendly_explanation: Garbage In, Garbage Out means if you put bad information into a computer program, the program will give you bad results. It's like if you mix up ingredients in a recipe; the dish won't turn out right.
example: If you enter wrong numbers into a calculator, it might give you a wrong answer, just like when you spill water on a map and can't read the directions.

formal_definition: A defined set of rules that governs how data is formatted, transmitted, and received between devices on a network, ensuring different systems can communicate reliably.
student_friendly_explanation: A protocol is like a set of instructions that tells computers how to talk to each other over the internet. It's important because it helps different types of computers understand each other and share information.
example: When you use a web browser to visit a website, the HTTP protocol is used to send requests from your computer to the server hosting the website.

formal_definition: A linear data structure that follows the First-In-First-Out (FIFO) principle, where elements are added at one end and removed from the other.
student_friendly_explanation: A queue is like a line where people wait to get served. You can only add people to the back of the line and remove them from the front. It's similar to how you might use a ticket line at an event.
example: When you're waiting for your turn on a ride at an amusement park, you join the line at the back and leave when it's your turn.

formal_definition: A measure of the amount of time an algorithm takes to run as a function of the size of its input, commonly expressed using Big O notation.
student_friendly_explanation: Time Complexity is how long an algorithm takes to run, depending on the size of the data it processes. We use Big O notation to describe this, which helps us understand and compare different algorithms.
example: Sorting a list of names alphabetically; the time it takes grows faster as the number of names increases.
related_terms: Big O Notation; Space Complexity; Algorithm Efficiency

formal_definition: A sequence of database operations that are treated as a single logical unit of work, either completing entirely or not at all, to preserve data consistency.
student_friendly_explanation: A transaction is like a series of steps you take when buying something from a store. These steps must all happen together or none of them do, to make sure your money and item are correctly handled.
example: When you buy a book online, the transaction includes adding the book to your cart, checking out, and receiving the confirmation email. If any step fails, the entire process doesn't complete.

formal_definition: An ordered, typically immutable collection of elements, which may be of different types, commonly used to group related values together.
student_friendly_explanation: A tuple is like a list of items where the order matters and each item can be different types. It's used to keep related pieces of information together.
example: You might use a tuple to store a person's name and age, like ('Alice', 30).

formal_definition: A software testing method where individual components or functions of a program are tested in isolation to verify that each performs as expected.
student_friendly_explanation: Unit Testing is like checking if each toy works properly before putting all toys together in a big playset. We test small parts of a computer program to make sure they do what they're supposed to do.
example: Imagine you have a function that adds two numbers. Unit Testing would check if adding 1 and 2 gives 3, just like how you'd test if a toy car runs smoothly.

formal_definition: Uniform Resource Locator, a reference that specifies the location of a resource on the internet along with the protocol used to access it, such as https.
student_friendly_explanation: A URL is like a special address that tells computers where to find information on the internet, just like how you use a house number to find a house.
example: When you type 'https://www.example.com' into your web browser, it's using a URL to connect to the website and show you its content.

formal_definition: The space where interactions between humans and a machine occur, encompassing the visual elements, layouts, and controls a user interacts with.
student_friendly_explanation: The User Interface is like the face of a computer or app that lets you talk to it. It includes things like buttons, menus, and screens you see when using a device.
example: A smartphone's home screen with icons for apps like Facebook, Maps, and Weather.

formal_definition: A system that records changes to files over time, allowing developers to track revisions, collaborate, and revert to previous versions when needed, such as Git.
student_friendly_explanation: Version control is like keeping a diary of all the changes you make to your favorite storybook. It helps you keep track of what you've written, who wrote it, and when, so you can go back to earlier versions if you need to.
example: A software developer uses version control to manage updates to a website, saving different versions of the code to ensure they can always go back to a working version if something goes wrong.
related_terms: Revision Control; Source Code Management; Revision History

formal_definition: The smallest sequence of programmed instructions that can be managed independently by a scheduler, typically existing as part of a larger process.
student_friendly_explanation: A thread is like a tiny worker inside a bigger program. It's a small piece of code that can run on its own while the main program is working on something else. Think of it as a helper that can do tasks without waiting for the main program to finish.
example: When you play a game and see multiple characters moving around the screen, each character might be running on its own thread so they can move smoothly without slowing down the game.

formal_definition: A software-based emulation of a physical computer, capable of running an operating system and applications as if it were a separate physical machine.
student_friendly_explanation: A virtual machine is like a pretend computer that runs inside another computer. It can run its own operating system and programs, just like a real computer would.
example: Virtual machines are used to test new software or run different operating systems without needing multiple physical computers.

formal_definition: Virtual Private Network, a technology that creates a secure, encrypted connection over a public network, allowing users to send and receive data as if directly connected.
student_friendly_explanation: A Virtual Private Network (VPN) is like a secret tunnel on the internet that helps keep your online activities safe and private by making them look like they're coming from another place.
example: When you use a VPN to connect to a website, it hides your real IP address and makes your internet traffic look like it's coming from somewhere else, like a different country.

formal_definition: A linear, sequential approach to software development where each phase, such as requirements, design, implementation, and testing, must be completed before the next begins.
student_friendly_explanation: The Waterfall Model is like building a house step-by-step: first you plan (requirements), then you draw blueprints (design), then you build the walls and roof (implementation), and finally you check everything works (testing). Each step has to be done completely before moving on.
example: A company developing a new mobile app would use the Waterfall Model to ensure that all features are planned and designed before coding begins, and then tested thoroughly before release.
related_terms: Requirement Gathering; Design Document; Code Review

formal_definition: Software or hardware that serves content, typically web pages, to clients over the internet using protocols such as HTTP, responding to browser requests.
student_friendly_explanation: A web server is like a big helper on the internet that gives out web pages and other information when you ask for them, just like how a librarian gives you books.
example: When you type a website's address into your browser, the web server sends back the page you want to see.

formal_definition: An access control mechanism that permits only explicitly approved items, such as email addresses or applications, while blocking everything else by default.
student_friendly_explanation: A whitelist is like a list of friends you allow into your house. In computer security, it's a list of apps and emails that are allowed to do things on your device, while everything else is blocked by default.
example: When you set up a new email account, you might add it to your whitelist so it can receive and send messages without being blocked.

formal_definition: Extensible Markup Language, a markup language designed to store and transport structured data in a format that is both human-readable and machine-readable.
student_friendly_explanation: XML is like a special set of rules for describing information, kind of like how you might write down instructions for assembling a toy. It helps computers understand and share data easily.
example: When you fill out a form on a website, the information you enter can be sent in XML format so that the website knows what you're trying to do.

formal_definition: A human-readable data serialization format commonly used for configuration files, relying on indentation rather than brackets to represent structure.
student_friendly_explanation: YAML is a way to write data that looks like plain text and uses indentation to show how things are organized. It's often used to make configuration files easier to read.
example:
A YAML file might look like this:

name: Alice
age: 30
is_student: false

formal_definition: A software security flaw that is unknown to the vendor or has no available fix at the time it is discovered or exploited, leaving systems exposed until patched.
student_friendly_explanation: A zero-day vulnerability is like finding a secret door in a castle that no one knows about. Until someone discovers and closes the door, bad guys can sneak in and cause problems.
example: Imagine a toy car that suddenly stops working without anyone knowing why. This could be a zero-day vulnerability if no one has found out how to fix it yet.

formal_definition: The creation of a virtual version of a resource, such as a server, storage device, or network, allowing multiple virtual instances to run on shared physical hardware.
student_friendly_explanation: Virtualization is like creating pretend versions of computer parts that let many different programs run at once using the same physical machine. It's like having several pretend computers inside one real computer!
example: A cloud provider uses virtualization to give each customer their own 'virtual server' even though they're sharing the same physical servers.

formal_definition: A request for information from a database, typically written in a query language such as SQL, that specifies the data to retrieve, filter, or modify.
student_friendly_explanation: A query is like asking a computer to find specific information from a big list of data. You write a special sentence called SQL, which tells the computer what you want to know and how to find it.
example: To find all the books about animals in a library's database, you might write a query like 'SELECT * FROM books WHERE subject = 'animals''.

formal_definition: The foundational suite of communication protocols used to interconnect network devices on the internet, defining how data is packetized, addressed, and delivered.
student_friendly_explanation: TCP/IP is like a set of rules that computers use to talk to each other over the internet. It helps break down information into small packets, gives each packet a special address, and makes sure all the packets arrive safely at their destination.
example: When you watch a video on YouTube, TCP/IP works behind the scenes to send the video data from the server to your computer.

formal_definition: A linear data structure that follows the Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) principle, where the most recently added element is the first one removed.
student_friendly_explanation: A stack is like a stack of plates where you can only add or remove plates from the top. The last plate you put on is the first one you take off.
example: When using a printer, documents are added to the print queue and printed in the order they were added.

formal_definition: A flaw in a system where the outcome depends on the uncontrollable timing of events, such as multiple threads accessing shared data simultaneously in an unintended order.
student_friendly_explanation: Race conditions happen when different parts of a program try to change the same information at the same time, and the result is unpredictable because they don't know what each other will do.
example: Imagine two friends trying to decide which movie to watch. If they both call at the same time and one says 'I'll go if you choose', but the other has already chosen, it's like a race condition where the outcome depends on who calls first.

formal_definition: A programming technique in which a function calls itself to solve smaller instances of the same problem, continuing until a base case is reached.
student_friendly_explanation: Recursion is like a game where you keep solving the same problem but make it smaller each time until you can't make it smaller anymore. It's like climbing stairs; you climb to the next step and then go back down to start over, but each time you're on a lower step.
example: A common example of recursion is calculating the factorial of a number, where you multiply the number by the factorial of the number minus one, until you reach zero.

formal_definition: The process of restructuring existing computer code without changing its external behavior, done to improve readability, reduce complexity, or make future changes easier.
student_friendly_explanation: Refactoring is like tidying up your room—changing how things look and work without changing what they do. It helps make your code cleaner and easier to understand.
example: Rewriting a long function into smaller, more manageable functions to improve its readability.

formal_definition: A type of software testing performed to confirm that recent code changes have not adversely affected existing features that previously worked correctly.
student_friendly_explanation: Regression testing is like checking if your favorite toy still works after you've added new parts. It makes sure that when you make small changes, important features don't stop working.
example: Imagine you're building a game and add a new feature to move characters. Regression testing helps ensure that the old way of moving characters (like jumping or running) still works properly.

formal_definition: A database that organizes data into tables of rows and columns, with relationships between tables defined through keys, typically queried using SQL.
student_friendly_explanation: A relational database is like organizing information into tables where each table has rows and columns. These tables are connected through special links called keys, and we use a language called SQL to ask the database questions and get answers.
example: Imagine you have a database of customers and orders. Each customer can place multiple orders, so we organize customers in one table and orders in another, linking them together using their unique IDs.

formal_definition: An architectural style for designing networked applications, relying on stateless communication and standard HTTP methods to allow systems to interact over the web.
student_friendly_explanation: Rest is like a set of rules for making sure different computer programs can talk to each other easily over the internet using simple commands.
example: When you use a website to order something online, the website uses Rest to send requests to the store's server to place the order.

formal_definition: An application programming interface that follows REST principles, allowing clients to access and manipulate resources through standard HTTP requests like GET and POST.
student_friendly_explanation: REST API is like a special language that lets computers talk to each other over the internet using simple commands like 'get' (to ask for something) and 'post' (to send something). It's how websites share information with apps.
example: When you search for something on Google, your device sends a request to Google's servers using REST API, which then fetches the results and sends them back to your device.

formal_definition: A type-checking approach in which variable types are known and verified at compile time rather than at runtime, catching certain errors before the program runs.
student_friendly_explanation: Static typing is like making sure all your toys have labels on them before you play with them. This way, you can catch mistakes early when you're building your toy castle, instead of finding out later that you used a block where a car was supposed to be.
example: When you write a program and define a variable to hold a number, static typing ensures that you only put numbers into that variable, not strings or other types, preventing many bugs.

formal_definition: The process of analyzing a system, device, or piece of software to understand how it works, often without access to its original design documentation or source code.
student_friendly_explanation: Reverse engineering is like taking apart a toy to see how it works, but instead of toys, we look inside complex computer programs to understand how they function.
example: Decoding a proprietary software program to fix bugs without the original developer's source code.

formal_definition: The capability of a system to handle a growing amount of work, or its potential to be enlarged to accommodate that growth, by adding resources.
student_friendly_explanation: Scalability is like making a cake bigger without changing the recipe. When a computer system can handle more tasks by adding more computers or servers, we say it's scalable.
example: A website that grows in popularity and needs to serve more users without slowing down, so they add more servers to handle the extra load.
related_terms: Resource Management; Load Balancing; Horizontal Scaling

formal_definition: A programming language designed for automating tasks that would otherwise be performed manually, typically interpreted rather than compiled, such as Python or Bash.
student_friendly_explanation: A scripting language is like a special set of instructions that computers can understand to do things automatically, like making a website load faster or changing settings on a computer. It's different from regular programming languages because it's usually run directly without needing to be turned into machine code first.
example: Using Bash scripts to automate system updates on a server.

formal_definition: An extension of the World Wide Web that aims to make data understandable by machines, not just humans, through standards that describe relationships between data.
student_friendly_explanation: The Semantic Web is like giving instructions to a robot so it can understand and use information on the web, making it easier for computers to communicate with each other.
example: When you search for recipes on the web and the search engine understands the ingredients and steps involved, it's using principles of the Semantic Web.

formal_definition: A computer program or device that provides functionality, data, or services to other programs or devices, called clients, typically over a network.
student_friendly_explanation: A server is like a helper computer on the internet that gives information or services to other computers, which we call clients. It's like when you ask a librarian for a book; the librarian is the server and the book is the service.
example: When you use Google to search for something, your computer (client) sends a request to Google’s servers, which then provide the search results.

formal_definition: A structured process that outlines the stages involved in developing software, from initial planning and design through implementation, testing, deployment, and maintenance.
student_friendly_explanation: The Software Development Life Cycle is like a recipe for making computer programs. It includes steps like planning what to make, drawing a blueprint, building the program, checking if it works, and then fixing any bugs before it's ready to use.
example: Creating a new app on your phone follows the Software Development Life Cycle. First, you decide what features it should have; then, you write down how everything will work; next, you build the app; after that, you test it to see if it works correctly; and finally, you fix any problems before users can download it.

formal_definition: An algorithm that arranges elements of a list or array in a particular order, typically numerical or lexicographical, such as quicksort, mergesort, or bubble sort.
student_friendly_explanation: A sorting algorithm is like a recipe for organizing a bunch of toys into neat piles. Just like how you might sort your toys alphabetically or by size, computer programs use sorting algorithms to arrange data in specific orders.
example: Imagine you have a list of names and you want to organize them alphabetically. A sorting algorithm helps your computer do this efficiently.

formal_definition: Structured Query Language, a standard programming language used to manage and manipulate relational databases, allowing users to query, insert, update, and delete data.
student_friendly_explanation: Structured Query Language, or SQL, is like a special set of instructions that helps you talk to and work with databases, which are like big collections of information. With SQL, you can ask questions about the data, add new information, change existing data, and even remove old data.
example: You might use SQL to find out how many people are older than 30 in a database of customer records.
related_terms: Database; Relational Database; Database Management System

formal_definition: The period during which a program is actively executing, as well as the environment or system that supports a program's execution, managing memory and resources.
student_friendly_explanation: Runtime is the time when a computer program is running and using the computer's resources like memory and CPU. It includes how the OS manages these resources to keep the program working smoothly.
example: When you play a video game, the runtime is when the game is actively running on your computer.
related_terms: Process Management; Memory Management; CPU Scheduling

formal_definition: A programming paradigm that treats computation as the evaluation of mathematical functions and avoids changing-state and mutable data.
student_friendly_explanation: Functional Programming is like solving puzzles where you use functions to transform inputs into outputs without changing anything outside the function. It's about doing things mathematically, making code easier to understand and less prone to errors.
example: Calculating factorial using recursion in a functional style, such as `factorial(n) = n * factorial(n-1)` if `n > 0`, with `factorial(0) = 1`.
related_terms: Lambda Calculus; Higher-order Functions; Pure Functions

formal_definition: A logical subdivision of an IP network, used to split a larger network into smaller, more manageable segments for organizational or performance reasons.
student_friendly_explanation: A subnet is like dividing a big playground into smaller areas so that kids can play in different sections without mixing up. It helps keep things organized and makes it easier to manage.
example: Imagine you have a big network of computers in a school. You might divide this network into smaller subnets based on different classes or grades to make it easier to control access and manage traffic.
related_terms: IP Address; CIDR Notation; Network Mask

formal_definition: A control flow statement for specifying iteration, which allows code to be executed repeatedly.
student_friendly_explanation: A for loop is like a set of instructions that tells a computer to do something over and over again, but you decide how many times.
example: You might use a for loop to print out all the numbers from 1 to 10.

formal_definition: Expressions of what the resource usage is at least, at most, and on average, respectively, for a given algorithm. Best case is the function which performs the minimum number of steps; worst case performs the maximum number of steps; average case performs an average number of steps.
student_friendly_explanation: Best, worst, and average case are different ways we describe how well an algorithm works. The best case means the algorithm does its job quickly with the least amount of work. The worst case is when the algorithm has to do more work than usual. And the average case is like when you do something halfway - neither too fast nor too slow.
example: Imagine sorting a list of numbers. In the best case, if the list is already sorted, the algorithm can finish very quickly. But in the worst case, if the list is completely mixed up, it might take longer to sort. The average case is when the list is somewhere in between.

formal_definition: A term used to refer to data sets that are too large or complex for traditional data-processing application software to adequately deal with.
student_friendly_explanation: Big Data refers to very large and complex datasets that can't be easily managed using standard tools. It's like having so much information that you need special software to handle it.
example: A hospital might use Big Data to analyze patient records and medical images to improve treatment methods and predict disease outbreaks.

formal_definition: A mathematical notation that describes the limiting behavior of a function when the argument tends towards a particular value or infinity.
student_friendly_explanation: Big O Notation is a way to describe how long an algorithm takes to run, especially as the size of its input gets very large. It helps us understand how the running time grows with the size of the data.
example: If you have a list of numbers and want to find the largest one, using a loop to check each number can be described with Big O Notation to show how quickly it will run as the list gets longer.
related_terms: Asymptotic Analysis; Theta Notation; Omega Notation

formal_definition: In mathematics and digital electronics, a number expressed in the base-2 numeral system, which uses only two symbols: typically 0 and 1.
student_friendly_explanation: A binary number is a way to represent numbers using just two digits: 0 and 1. It's like counting with only two fingers!
example: The decimal number 5 is represented as binary as 101.
related_terms: Decimal Number; Hexadecimal Number; Binary Code

formal_definition: A search algorithm that finds the position of a target value within a sorted array.
student_friendly_explanation: The Binary Search Algorithm is like playing hide and seek in a sorted list. Instead of looking everywhere, you start in the middle and keep checking the left or right half based on whether the target number is bigger or smaller than what you found. This way, you can find the number much faster than searching through the whole list.
example: Imagine you have a sorted list of exam scores from lowest to highest, and you want to find out if John's score is in there. Using the Binary Search Algorithm, you'd quickly narrow down where John's score could be without checking every single score.

formal_definition: A tree data structure in which each node has at most two children, referred to as the left child and the right child.
student_friendly_explanation: A binary tree is like a family tree where each person can have at most two children - a younger brother or sister on the left, and a younger sister or brother on the right.
example: The file directory structure on your computer can be represented as a binary tree, with folders being the nodes and subfolders being the children.

formal_definition: An interdisciplinary field that combines biology, computer science, information engineering, mathematics, and statistics to develop methods and software tools for analyzing and interpreting biological data.
student_friendly_explanation: Bioinformatics is like using computers to help scientists understand big sets of genetic information. It's where biology meets computer science to solve complex problems in genetics.
example: Scientists use bioinformatics tools to compare DNA sequences from different species to find similarities and differences.

formal_definition: The act of running a computer program, a set of programs, or other operations, in order to assess the relative performance of an object, normally by running a number of standard tests and trials against it.
student_friendly_explanation: Benchmarking is like testing how fast your toy car runs on different surfaces to see which surface makes it go the fastest. In computing, we do this to see how well different computers or software perform.
example: A company might use benchmarking to find out which of two new processors is faster at handling tasks.

formal_definition: A basic unit of information used in computing and digital communications; a portmanteau of binary digit. A binary digit can have one of two possible values.
student_friendly_explanation: A bit is like a tiny switch that can be either on or off, representing a piece of information. It's used to store numbers and letters in computers.
example: When you type a letter on your keyboard, each letter is stored using bits.

formal_definition: In computing, a basic access control mechanism that allows through all elements except those explicitly mentioned in a list of prohibited elements.
student_friendly_explanation: A blacklist is like a list of bad guys you don't want to let into a game. In computing, it's a way to stop unwanted things from coming into a system or network.
example: When you play a game and have a list of banned players, that's similar to how a blacklist works in computers to block certain types of data.

formal_definition: A data type that has one of two possible values, usually denoted true and false, intended to represent the two truth values of logic and Boolean algebra.
student_friendly_explanation: Boolean data type is like a special kind of box that can only hold two types of things: true or false. It's used in programming to make decisions based on whether something is true or not.
example: A simple example could be a program that checks if a number is even or odd, using true for even and false for odd.

formal_definition: An expression used in a programming language that returns a Boolean value when evaluated, that is one of true or false.
student_friendly_explanation: A Boolean expression is like a yes-or-no question in computer code that tells the program whether something is true or false.
example: The condition 'age > 18' is a Boolean expression that checks if someone is old enough to vote.
related_terms: Programming Language; Conditional Statement; Logical Operator

formal_definition: In mathematics and mathematical logic, the branch of algebra in which the values of the variables are the truth values true and false.
student_friendly_explanation: Boolean Algebra is like a special kind of math used to work with true or false values, just like flipping a light switch on or off. It's used in computers to make decisions and solve problems.
example: A simple example could be using a light switch that turns on when you press a button (true) and off when you don't (false).
related_terms: Logic Gates; Set Theory; Truth Tables

formal_definition: A unit of digital information that most commonly consists of eight bits, representing a binary number. Historically it was the number of bits used to encode a single character of text.
student_friendly_explanation: A byte is like a group of 8 smaller units called bits that together can represent a letter or number. It's how computers store and understand information.
example: When you type a message on your computer, each letter is broken down into bytes so the computer can understand and display it correctly.

formal_definition: The procedures implemented in starting up a computer or computer appliance until it can be used. It can be initiated by hardware such as a button press or by a software command.
student_friendly_explanation: Booting is like turning on a computer and making sure all its parts work together so you can use it. It's like asking a sleepy friend to wake up and start playing.
example: When you turn on your computer and see the colorful startup screen before Windows loads, that's booting.

formal_definition: Any executable code that is passed as an argument to other code that is expected to call back and execute the argument at a given time.
student_friendly_explanation: A callback is like asking a friend to do something for you later, but instead of waiting, you give them instructions now and they will do it when they're ready.
example: In a game, you might ask a helper function to check if the player has won after each move, and it will do so when called.

formal_definition: In telecommunications and computing, the number of bits that are conveyed or processed per unit of time.
student_friendly_explanation: Bit rate is how many bits of information can be sent through a network in a second. It's like measuring how fast you can send messages on a phone line.
example: When you watch a video online, the bit rate determines how quickly the video streams to your computer.
related_terms: Bandwidth; Data Transfer Rate; Transmission Speed

formal_definition: The electronic circuitry within a computer that carries out the instructions of a computer program by performing the basic arithmetic, logic, controlling, and input/output operations specified by the instructions.
student_friendly_explanation: The Central Processing Unit (CPU) is like the brain of a computer. It's the part that tells all the other parts what to do, just like how you tell your body what to do.
example: When you play a video game, the CPU helps process all the graphics and actions on the screen.

formal_definition: A formalism and a methodology for having a technique to specify probabilistic models and solve problems when less than the necessary information is available.
student_friendly_explanation: Bayesian Programming is a way to create models that can make predictions even when we don't have all the information. It's like guessing what you might wear based on the weather forecast and your mood, even if you haven't checked the weather today.
example: Predicting the weather where you live using past data and current conditions, even if you've never seen the exact same weather combination before.
related_terms: Machine Learning; Probability Theory; Statistical Inference

formal_definition: An area of computer science and mathematical logic dedicated to understanding different aspects of reasoning. The study of automated reasoning helps produce computer programs that allow computers to reason completely, or nearly completely, automatically.
student_friendly_explanation: Automated reasoning is about making computers think like humans do, but faster and without getting tired. It's like teaching a computer how to solve problems using rules and logic, so it can figure things out on its own.
example: A chatbot that can understand and respond to complex questions by using automated reasoning techniques.
related_terms: Logic Programming; Knowledge Representation; Expert Systems

formal_definition: The act of proving or disproving the correctness of intended algorithms underlying a system with respect to a certain formal specification, using formal methods of mathematics.
student_friendly_explanation: Formal Verification is like double-checking a recipe to make sure all the steps work correctly before you start cooking. It's used to ensure computer systems do what they're supposed to do without any mistakes.
example: Verifying that a traffic light controller works perfectly under all conditions to avoid red lights when cars are not present.

formal_definition: One with only a signature and no implementation body. It is often used to specify that a subclass must provide an implementation of the method. Abstract methods are used to specify interfaces in some computer languages.
student_friendly_explanation: An abstract method is like a blueprint for a method that doesn't have its own code but tells other classes what it should do. It's used when you want other classes to write their own version of the method.
example: Imagine you're building a car class hierarchy where you want all cars to have a 'startEngine' method. Instead of writing the same code for each type of car, you can make 'startEngine' an abstract method so that each car subclass has to write its own version of how to start the engine.

formal_definition: In software engineering and computer science, the process of removing physical, spatial, or temporal details or attributes in the study of objects or systems in order to more closely attend to other details of interest; it is also very similar in nature to the process of generalization. The result of this process is an abstract concept-object created by keeping common features or attributes to various concrete objects or systems of study.
student_friendly_explanation: Abstraction is like when you look at a big toy box full of different toys and focus on just the fun parts without worrying about how they're made or where they came from.
example: When you use a credit card, you don't need to know how the bank processes transactions; you just use the abstraction that makes payments easy.

formal_definition: A blueprint for software agents and intelligent control systems depicting the arrangement of components. The architectures implemented by intelligent agents are referred to as cognitive architectures.
student_friendly_explanation: Agent Architecture is like a blue-print for smart robots or computer programs that can think and act on their own. It shows how different parts of the system work together to make decisions and perform tasks.
example: A chatbot that can understand and respond to human conversations uses agent architecture to process language and provide appropriate responses.
related_terms: Software Agent; Intelligent Control System; Cognitive Architecture

formal_definition: A class of computational models for simulating the actions and interactions of autonomous agents with a view to assessing their effects on the system as a whole. It combines elements of game theory, complex systems, emergence, computational sociology, multi-agent systems, and evolutionary programming.
student_friendly_explanation: An Agent-Based Model is like playing a big game where each player (or 'agent') makes decisions based on simple rules. We watch how all the players interact and change the game's outcome together.
example: Simulating how different types of ants work together to build their nests.

formal_definition: In database management, a function in which the values of multiple rows are grouped together to form a single value of more significant meaning or measurement, such as a sum, count, or max.
student_friendly_explanation: An aggregate function is like when you add up all the numbers in a group of friends' ages to find out how old everyone is on average.
example: If you have a table of sales data and you want to know the total sales amount, you would use an aggregate function to add up all the sales figures.

formal_definition: An approach to software development under which requirements and solutions evolve through the collaborative effort of self-organizing and cross-functional teams and their customers or end users. It advocates adaptive planning, evolutionary development, early delivery, and continual improvement, and it encourages rapid and flexible response to change.
student_friendly_explanation: Agile Software Development is like building a big sandcastle with your friends. Instead of planning every detail first, you work together, make changes as you go, and keep improving based on what you learn.
example: A team of developers working on a mobile app that needs to be updated quickly to meet changing user preferences.

formal_definition: The maximum rate of data transfer across a given path. Bandwidth may be characterized as network bandwidth, data bandwidth, or digital bandwidth.
student_friendly_explanation: Bandwidth is like the speed limit on a highway for data. It tells us how fast information can travel through a network, whether it's the internet or a local computer system.
example: When you watch a high-definition video stream, the bandwidth required to do so depends on the quality and resolution of the video.
related_terms: Data Transfer Rate; Transmission Speed; Network Capacity

formal_definition: An unambiguous specification of how to solve a class of problems. Algorithms can perform calculation, data processing, and automated reasoning tasks. They are ubiquitous in computing technologies.
student_friendly_explanation: An algorithm is like a recipe for solving a problem. It's a step-by-step guide that tells a computer what to do, just like you follow a recipe to bake a cake.
example: Sorting numbers in a list, where you take a bunch of numbers and arrange them in order from smallest to largest.

formal_definition: A property of an algorithm which relates to the number of computational resources used by the algorithm. An algorithm must be analyzed to determine its resource usage, and the efficiency of an algorithm can be measured based on usage of different resources.
student_friendly_explanation: Algorithmic efficiency is about how well an algorithm uses computer resources like time and space. We measure this to make sure our programs run fast and use little memory.
example: Sorting a large list of numbers efficiently so that we can find the highest or lowest number quickly.
related_terms: Time Complexity; Space Complexity; Big O Notation

formal_definition: Computer software designed to perform a group of coordinated functions, tasks, or activities for the benefit of the user. Common examples include word processors, spreadsheets, accounting applications, web browsers, media players, and photo editors.
student_friendly_explanation: Application software is like special tools you use on your computer to do specific jobs, like writing stories, organizing numbers, or playing games. It's different from system software that helps your computer work better.
example: A word processor lets you write and edit documents easily.

formal_definition: A data structure consisting of a collection of elements, each identified by at least one array index or key. An array is stored such that the position of each element can be computed from its index tuple by a mathematical formula.
student_friendly_explanation: An array is like a list where you can store items, and each item has a special number called an index to find it quickly.
example: You can use an array to keep track of scores in a game, where each player's score is stored at a specific position in the array.

formal_definition: Intelligence demonstrated by machines, in contrast to the natural intelligence displayed by humans and other animals. AI research is defined as the study of intelligent agents, devices capable of perceiving their environment and taking actions that maximize the chance of successfully achieving their goals.
student_friendly_explanation: Artificial Intelligence is like giving computers the ability to think and learn, just like how you use your brain to solve problems. It's about making machines do smart things, like recognizing faces or playing games.
example: Self-driving cars use AI to understand traffic and make decisions on the road.

formal_definition: In computer programming, a statement that a predicate is always true at that point in code execution. It can help a programmer read the code, help a compiler compile it, or help the program detect its own defects.
student_friendly_explanation: An assertion is like a promise you make to yourself or your computer about something being true. It helps programmers check if their code works correctly and can catch mistakes before the program runs.
example: If you write a program that checks if a number is even, you might use an assertion to say 'This number should be even,' which helps ensure your program doesn't have bugs.

formal_definition: An associative array, map, symbol table, or dictionary is an abstract data type composed of a collection of key-value pairs, such that each possible key appears at most once in the collection.
student_friendly_explanation: An associative array is like a magical box where you can store things using names instead of numbers. Each name points to something, and you can quickly find what you're looking for.
example: A phone book where names are keys and phone numbers are values.

formal_definition: The study of abstract machines and automata, as well as the computational problems that can be solved using them. It is a theory in theoretical computer science and discrete mathematics.
student_friendly_explanation: Automata Theory is like studying different types of robots that can follow rules to solve problems. It's important in understanding how computers work and how we design them.
example: Imagine you have a vending machine that only accepts certain coins. Automata Theory helps us understand how such machines work and how they can be designed.

formal_definition: A method or mathematical process for problem-solving and for engineering algorithms. The design of algorithms is part of many solution theories of operation research, such as dynamic programming and divide-and-conquer.
student_friendly_explanation: An algorithm is like a recipe for solving problems using steps that a computer can follow. It's how we tell computers what to do, and it's used in many areas of computer science.
example: Sorting a list of numbers from smallest to largest is a common algorithm you might use every day when organizing your shopping list.
related_terms: Data Structures; Programming Fundamentals; Software Engineering

formal_definition: A unit of information that roughly corresponds to a grapheme, grapheme-like unit, or symbol, such as in an alphabet or syllabary in the written form of a natural language.
student_friendly_explanation: A character is like a single letter or symbol you see in words and sentences. It's a basic building block of text in computers.
example: When you type 'A' on your keyboard, it sends a character to the computer.

formal_definition: A set of subroutine definitions, communication protocols, and tools for building software. In general terms, it is a set of clearly defined methods of communication among various components. A good API makes it easier to develop a computer program by providing all the building blocks.
student_friendly_explanation: An API is like a recipe book for computer programs. It tells you how to make different parts of a program work together smoothly, making it easier for developers to build apps without starting from scratch.
example: When you use a map app on your phone, the API between the app and the GPS system allows the app to show you directions.

formal_definition: In object-oriented programming, an extensible program-code-template for creating objects, providing initial values for state and implementations of behavior.
student_friendly_explanation: A class is like a blueprint for making objects. It tells you how to create things that can do certain actions and have specific states.
example: When you design a car, the class would be the blueprint that defines what a car looks like and how it works.

formal_definition: The order in which individual statements, instructions or function calls of an imperative program are executed or evaluated.
student_friendly_explanation: Control Flow is like following a recipe to bake cookies. Just as you follow each step in the right order to make the perfect cookie, a computer follows instructions in a specific sequence to perform tasks.
example: When you press 'Enter' on a form, the system checks if the input is correct before moving to the next field, demonstrating control flow.

formal_definition: The practice and study of techniques for secure communication in the presence of third parties called adversaries, including data confidentiality, data integrity, authentication, and non-repudiation.
student_friendly_explanation: Cryptography is like a secret code we use to keep messages safe from bad guys who might try to read them. It helps us make sure our information stays private and can't be changed without us knowing.
example: When you log into your favorite website, cryptography makes sure that only you can see your password and that no one else can peek at it.

formal_definition: A process of discovering patterns in large data sets involving methods at the intersection of machine learning, statistics, and database systems.
student_friendly_explanation: Data mining is like finding hidden treasures in a big pile of information. It uses special tools to look for interesting patterns that can help us understand things better.
example: Finding out which products customers are most likely to buy based on their shopping history.

formal_definition: An interdisciplinary field that uses scientific methods, processes, algorithms, and systems to extract knowledge and insights from data in various forms, structured and unstructured.
student_friendly_explanation: Data Science is like solving puzzles with numbers and information. It helps us find hidden patterns in big sets of data using special tools and techniques.
example: A company might use Data Science to understand customer preferences and improve their products.

formal_definition: A data organization, management, and storage format that enables efficient access and modification, comprising a collection of data values, relationships, and applicable operations.
student_friendly_explanation: A data structure is like a special way to organize your toys so you can find them easily and play with them quickly. It helps computers store information in a smart way.
example: Imagine you have a toy box where you keep all your action figures. Each figure has a name tag. Using a data structure, you could make it easier to find your favorite figure by sorting them alphabetically or grouping them by color.

formal_definition: An attribute of data which tells the compiler or interpreter how the programmer intends to use the data, constraining the values an expression might take.
student_friendly_explanation: A data type is like telling a computer what kind of information you're dealing with, whether it's numbers, words, or dates, so the computer knows how to handle it correctly.
example: When you declare a variable to store a number, you specify its data type as 'integer' or 'float', which tells the computer how much space to reserve and how to interpret the value.

formal_definition: The process of finding and resolving defects or problems within a computer program that prevent correct operation of computer software or the system as a whole.
student_friendly_explanation: Debugging is like fixing bugs in a storybook to make sure all characters can talk and move correctly. It's when we find mistakes in computer programs so they work properly.
example: Fixing a typo in a code that causes the program to crash when you try to use it.

formal_definition: The practice of integrating source code changes frequently and ensuring that an integrated codebase is in a workable state.
student_friendly_explanation: Continuous Integration is like making sure all the parts of a big project come together smoothly every time you add new pieces. It helps catch mistakes early and keeps everything working well.
example: A team of developers working on a web application use Continuous Integration to automatically test their code whenever someone makes a change, so they know if something breaks right away.
related_terms: Version Control; Automated Testing; Build Automation

formal_definition: In computer programming, a language construct that specifies properties of an identifier, declaring what a word means, most commonly for functions, variables, constants, and classes.
student_friendly_explanation: A declaration is like giving a name to something in your program, telling the computer what it is and how to use it. For example, you might declare a variable to hold a number or a function to do a specific task.
example: You might declare a variable named 'age' to store someone's age in a program.

formal_definition: A hierarchical and decentralized naming system for computers, services, or other resources connected to the internet or a private network, translating domain names to numerical IP addresses.
student_friendly_explanation: The Domain Name System (DNS) is like a phone book for the internet. It helps us remember website names instead of remembering long numbers called IP addresses.
example: When you type 'www.google.com' into your web browser, DNS translates this name into the number (IP address) that allows your computer to connect to Google's servers.
related_terms: IP Address; Internet Protocol; DNS Server

formal_definition: The process of encoding information, converting plaintext into an alternative form known as ciphertext so that only authorized parties can decipher it back to the original information.
student_friendly_explanation: Encryption is like turning your secret message into a code that only you and people with the right key can read. It's used to keep messages safe from others who shouldn't see them.
example: When you send an email with sensitive information, encryption makes sure that only the person you're sending it to can read the contents.

formal_definition: A programming paradigm in which the flow of the program is determined by events such as user actions, sensor outputs, or messages from other programs or threads.
student_friendly_explanation: Event-driven programming is like playing a game where you don't control the action; instead, things happen based on what players do or sensors detect. It's used to make computer programs respond to different events, like when you click a button or a doorbell rings.
example: A simple event-driven program could be a weather app that updates its display when the temperature changes.

formal_definition: The process of responding to the occurrence of exceptions, anomalous or exceptional conditions requiring special processing that often disrupt the normal flow of program execution.
student_friendly_explanation: Exception handling is like having a plan B when something unexpected happens during a computer program's work. It helps the program know what to do when errors occur.
example: When you try to divide a number by zero, exception handling can tell the program to alert the user and avoid crashing.

formal_definition: Causes a computer to perform indicated tasks according to encoded instructions, as opposed to a data file that must be parsed by a program to be meaningful.
student_friendly_explanation: An executable is like a set of instructions written in a special language that a computer can understand and follow directly. It's different from a regular file because it doesn't need to be translated into something else before it can run.
example: When you download and install a new app on your phone, the app's code is compiled into an executable file so your phone can run it without needing to decode it first.

formal_definition: In cryptography, an algorithm for performing encryption or decryption, a series of well-defined steps that can be followed as a procedure.
student_friendly_explanation: A cipher is like a secret code used to change messages so only people who know the right code can read them. It's part of how we keep our information safe online.
example: When you use a password to log into your favorite website, the website uses a cipher to make sure only you can access your account.

formal_definition: In a programming language, a combination of constants, variables, operators, and functions that the language interprets and computes to produce another value.
student_friendly_explanation: An expression is like a recipe in coding where you mix numbers, letters, symbols, and special commands to make the computer do something.
example: Calculating the area of a rectangle using length and width: `area = length * width`

formal_definition: A field of computer science that studies distributed systems, whose components are located on different networked computers that communicate and coordinate actions by passing messages.
student_friendly_explanation: Distributed computing is like having many friends spread out in different places who can work together to solve a big puzzle. Each friend has part of the puzzle, and they send pieces back and forth to complete the whole picture.
example: A large online game where players' actions are processed by servers located all over the world, allowing gamers to interact instantly regardless of their physical location.

formal_definition: Producing software in short cycles with high speed and frequency so that reliable software can be released at any time, with a simple and repeatable deployment process.
student_friendly_explanation: Continuous Delivery is like making sure you can quickly send out updates to your favorite app or game whenever you want, without any big problems. It's about making sure everything works smoothly every time.
